visual_features: Large hornbill 70-80 cm, males 2,360-2,500 g. Males have rufous/buff face and neck, orange-red eyes, prominent high red casque atop yellow bill, pale blue skin around eye, bare dark blue throat. Females have entirely black face and neck, yellow casque, brownish eyes. Both sexes have white tail feathers, blackish feet, large yellow bill. Juveniles resemble males with entirely yellow casqueless bill.
description: The knobbed hornbill (also known as Sulawesi wrinkled hornbill) is a colourful bird endemic to Indonesia, found only on Sulawesi and its offshore islands (Buton, Lembeh, Togian, Muna). It is the faunal symbol of South Sulawesi province. These iconic hornbills form long-term monogamous bonds and are highly vocal, using deep guttural calls to communicate across the forest. Primarily frugivorous, they play a vital role as seed dispersers in Sulawesi's rainforest ecosystems, particularly dependent on fig trees (Ficus spp.) as a keystone food source. Sometimes placed in genus Aceros.
population_estimate: Declining rapidly across Sulawesi. Between 1985-1997, 89% of lowland forests in Sulawesi were lost. Listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List with CITES Appendix II protection.
habitat: Evergreen lowland and montane rainforest at elevations up to 1,800 m. Also utilizes secondary forest, woodland, and plantations for foraging. Depends on large, mature old-growth trees (13-53 m high) for nesting cavities. Thrives in tall primary forests with abundant fig trees. Found on Sulawesi, Buton, Lembeh, Togian, and Muna Island.
threats: Rapid deforestation for palm oil plantations and rice fields
Commercial and illegal logging removing large nesting trees
Gold mining operations destroying primary forest on Buton
Hunting for bushmeat and casque ornaments
Fragmentation isolating populations and reducing breeding success
ecosystem_role: Knobbed hornbills are crucial seed dispersers in Sulawesi's rainforest ecosystems. They primarily eat fruits, especially figs, and disperse seeds across large distances through daily flights covering 30-60 km². Their foraging and seed dispersal influence the initial fate of seeds of several tropical forest tree species. As frugivores dependent on large-fruiting trees, their health reflects forest ecosystem integrity.
human_connection: The knobbed hornbill is the faunal symbol of South Sulawesi province, representing regional pride and biodiversity heritage. Valued in ecotourism for birdwatchers visiting Sulawesi's remaining forests. Hunted for bushmeat and their casques sold as ornaments despite legal protection. Dependence on large trees makes them an indicator species for forest health. First described by Coenraad Jacob Temminck in 1823.
what_students_can_do: Learn about the impact of palm oil deforestation on Indonesian endemic species
Support sustainable palm oil alternatives and boycott products linked to deforestation
Study hornbill ecology and seed dispersal mechanisms in tropical forests
Advocate for protection of Sulawesi's remaining lowland rainforests
Raise awareness about the illegal wildlife trade affecting hornbills
fun_fact: The female seals herself inside a tree hole with her own feces during egg-laying, leaving only a small slit through which the male passes food for the entire 27-30 week breeding season
Knobbed hornbills have been known to chase off other birds and even primates at fruiting trees, showing their dominance in the rainforest canopy
They can live up to 30 years in the wild, but successful breeding depends on stable territory and abundant fig trees
The species feeds on at least 35 plant species in 13 genera, with figs forming 60-85% of their diet depending on season
